title: I built a detective card game with Claude and Gemini. What worked, and what the playtest showed
author: DmitryTsepelev
selftext:
Ink & Evidence is a detective game where everything you learn lies on the table as cards. You question people about specific things, examine evidence and cross-reference facts. The game never confirms a deduction: you fill in the verdict yourself. The demo has one case and runs in the browser for free.
    
    
    How it was made:
    - I designed the game and the case. The code was written with Claude: Phaser and TypeScript.
    - A case is data. Cards carry aspects, actions have slots, and recipes match the cards in the slots. That made it possible for Claude to write and rewrite a case quickly, and for tests to check it.
    - The hard part was not the code but the case. I keep a written guide of what makes a case fair: every card must change a decision, a decoy must be believable, and the truth must not give itself away by where a card comes from. The tests enforce what can be enforced. For example, every rebuttal names at most two cards, and every first move gives a card or a hint.
    - The illustrations were made with Gemini. For the animated intro I generated cut-out figures on a flat green background, keyed them out, and moved them like a paper theatre in the browser.
    
    
    For a playtest I collected turns to the Google sheet and added a small tool  that replays every game on the current code. As a result, I was able to fix a bunch of common confusion sources:
    - The most common first move was examining the body, and it gave nothing. Now it gives a card.
    - One player pressed End turn three times with nothing on the actions and lost three hours of game time. Now an empty turn does not pass.
    - Most failed accusations got the time of death wrong. Now the first failed accusation sends the case back with one reason, instead of ending the game.
